old: London was shaken by a crime of such singular ferocity, and made all the more notorious by the high standing of the victim, that the details were few but startling.
new: London was shaken by a crime of singular ferocity, made all the more notable by the high standing of the victim. The details were few and startling.
reason: Source: ‘startled by a crime of singular ferocity and rendered all the more notable by the high position of the victim. The details were few and startling.’ The candidate’s ‘such … that’ adds a false cause (the ferocity made the details few), and ‘notorious’ changes ‘notable’.

old: the self-possession of a man well satisfied with himself
new: as of a man with good reason to be satisfied with himself
reason: Source ‘as of a well-founded self-content’: the self-content is justified; ‘well satisfied with himself’ loses ‘well-founded’ and can sound smug, which undercuts the portrait of the victim.

new: let out a sigh he could not hold back
reason: Source ‘heaved an irrepressible sigh’ means a sigh he could not suppress, not a reluctant one.
House style is British: ‘practising’ (source spelling too).

old: had already had their foot on the threshold
new: already had their foot on the threshold
reason: ‘once … had already had their foot’ is an awkward tense when read aloud; source ‘had already their foot on the threshold’.

old: a darkness came over his eyes
new: a darkness came around his eyes
reason: Source ‘there came a blackness about his eyes’ means shadows around the eyes, not his eyes clouding over.
House style is British and the source says ‘cheque book’; chapter 1 uses ‘cheque’ throughout, so ‘checkbook’ is inconsistent.
Same as 4.15: source ‘cheque book’, British style, matches ‘cheque’ in chapter 1.
Source ‘the plate was of silver’ says what the tableware was made of (solid silver, not plated), not that it was ‘fine’.

old: He doesn’t seem a very popular man
new: He don’t seem a very popular man
reason: Source ‘He don’t seem a very popular character’: the inspector’s colloquial grammar is part of his voice and separates him from the gentlemen; standardising it flattens him.
‘Up your alley’ is American; the British idiom fits the house style and the speaker (source ‘quite in your way’).

old: the ordinary kind of doctor of the day— no particular age
new: the ordinary kind of doctor of the day—of no particular age
reason: Stray space after the em dash (the only one in chs 1–5); restoring ‘of’ makes the phrase grammatical again (source ‘of no particular age and colour’).

The source’s ‘cabinet’ becomes ‘study’ here and in ch 8, but chs 6, 9 and 10 of the candidate keep ‘cabinet’ with no gloss (e.g. 6.12 ‘the cabinet above the laboratory’, 9.3 ‘The door of my cabinet is then to be forced’). Naming both terms at the first mention lets a first-time listener tell that the room is not a piece of furniture.
